statement: In people who use ketamine and other drugs, studied by one research group at University College London, frequent ketamine use compared with no ketamine use is associated with more delusion-like (unusual) beliefs, more dissociation in everyday life and somewhat more depressive symptoms, which the authors call mild to moderate in one study and below clinical levels in two others; whether ketamine causes these differences is unknown. In one session (Morgan et al., 2009; groups of 30), people who used ketamine more than four times a week scored higher than 30 people who used other drugs and 30 who used no illicit drugs on a delusions inventory (22.72 against 13.03 and 9.43), on unusual experiences in daily life when not under the influence of drugs, on a dissociative experiences scale (784 against 488 and 321) and on a depression inventory (11.48 against 7.17 and 7.23, which the authors call mild to moderate depression); the editors could reproduce the differences from both control groups for delusions and dissociation, but for depression only the difference from the group who had stopped. People who used ketamine less often (at least monthly but less than four times a week) or had stopped scored between the frequent and non-drug groups on several of these scales, but their reported excess of delusional ideation over the non-drug group could not be reproduced from the printed table. A year later (Morgan et al., 2010b; the same people), delusional ideation (8.39 and 8.04 items endorsed in the frequent group, against 5.63 and 4.50 in the polydrug and 3.90 and 3.95 in the non-drug group) and dissociation were still highest in the frequent group, while the groups who used ketamine less often or had stopped were also reported above the non-drug group on delusional ideation (P = 0.009 and 0.016); depression scores had risen in the frequent (7.08 to 10.67) and abstinent groups (4.96 to 9.00), the frequent group reported more negative life events over the year, and the first report gives the frequent group's depression score at the same first session as 11.48, so either the two reports disagree or the 5 people not retested averaged about 33. Three days after a night of use, a ketamine group that used ketamine from twice a week to once a month rated more dissociation (17.75 against 5.37) and psychosis-like experiences (62.35 against 26.42), on scales of how they felt at that moment, one of them built for the study, than peers with little or no ketamine use, and slightly higher depression scores on both test days, the first rating covering the two days up to the test on the night (Curran & Morgan, 2000); in a second sample, people who used ketamine more than twice a month and people who used it less did not differ in dissociation or psychosis-like scores three days after use (Curran & Monaghan, 2001). In 18 people who had cut down, retested after 3 to 4 years, psychosis-like (schizotypal) scores stayed higher than in 10 controls (18.67 against 4.0) and depression scores, measured only at follow-up, were higher (5.27 against 2.00, although the printed test, U = 55.5, gives p ≈ 0.10 on the editors' recalculation), while dissociation did not differ (Morgan et al., 2004a). The frequent group of the main study had more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 against 1 to 3) and less education; nobody was assessed before using ketamine, the measures are self-ratings, and no study read gives a rate of diagnosed psychotic illness (one person in the 3-year follow-up had developed schizophrenia and was excluded, a single case that gives no rate). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In one London team's studies, people who used ketamine more than four times a week reported more unusual beliefs, more moments of feeling detached from themselves or their surroundings in everyday life, and a little more low mood than people who used other drugs or none. On average, their low-mood scores were at most mild to moderate. A year later the same differences were there, and low mood had risen in the frequent group and in people who had stopped. People who used ketamine less often were in between on some of these scales. In two smaller studies that asked how people felt at that moment, three days after a night out, feeling detached was higher in one study but not in the other. The frequent group had more family members with mental illness and less schooling, and nobody was asked these questions before they started, so the studies cannot show that ketamine caused the differences.
population: People who use ketamine and other drugs, studied by one research group at University College London: five groups of 30 (119 retested a year later), two field samples recruited at parties, nightclubs and squat parties, and 18 of their participants retested after 3 to 4 years
exposure: Frequent ketamine use (more than four times a week in the main study), by self-report checked with hair analysis; less frequent use, past use and, in the field studies, use from once a month to twice a week
comparator: People who used other drugs but not ketamine and people who used no illicit drugs; in the field studies, peers with little or no ketamine use, or people who used ketamine twice a month or less
outcome: Self-rated delusion-like beliefs (Peters et al. Delusions Inventory), unusual experiences (O-LIFE), state schizotypal symptoms, dissociation (Dissociative Experiences Scale; an adapted dissociative states scale) and depressive symptoms (Beck Depression Inventory; Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale), rated when not intoxicated
magnitude: Morgan et al. (2009), groups of 30: delusions inventory total 22.72 (frequent) against 15.1 (infrequent), 15.79 (ex-ketamine), 13.03 (polydrug) and 9.43 (non-drug); dissociative experiences 784 against 630, 401, 488 and 321; Beck Depression Inventory 11.48 against 9.03, 6.00, 7.17 and 7.23 (only the difference from the ex-ketamine group reproduces, editors' recalculation); delusions with amount per session in the frequent group r = 0.433. Morgan et al. (2010b), same cohort one year later: delusions items 8.39 and 8.04 (frequent) against 5.63 and 4.50 (polydrug) and 3.90 and 3.95 (non-drug), with the infrequent and abstinent groups also above the non-drug group (P = 0.009 and 0.016); dissociation, frequent above both control groups (P = 0.015 and 0.009); depression 7.08 to 10.67 (frequent; 11.48 for all 30 at the same session in the 2009 report) and 4.96 to 9.00 (abstinent). Curran & Morgan (2000), 3 days after use, state ratings: dissociation 17.75 against 5.37, schizotypal 62.35 against 26.42; HADS depression 4.30 against 1.68 (and 4.45 against 1.89 for the two days up to the night). Curran & Monaghan (2001), 3 days after use: dissociation 4.56 against 3.47, schizotypal 25.28 against 28.95 (no difference). Morgan et al. (2004a), 18 against 10: schizotypal 51.5 against 24.8 and 18.67 against 4.0 (the controls' baseline 24.8 (8.16) is printed again, the same mean and SD, as the ketamine group's serial-sevens score in the Results, so one of the two may be a printing error; editors' observation); dissociation 10.11 against 5.44 and 3.24 against 0.80 (no difference); HADS depression at follow-up 5.27 against 2.00 (printed U = 55.5; two-tailed p ≈ 0.10, editors' recalculation).

evidence.locator: Assessments › Psychological wellbeing › O-LIFE (p. 79); Results › Self-report measures › O-LIFE, PDI and Dissociative experiences scale (p. 83); Table 6 (p. 84)
evidence.extracted: The O-LIFE questionnaire, whose unusual-experiences factor is described as akin to hallucinatory and delusional experiences, asks people to rate their current daily life when not under the influence of drugs. Unusual experiences: group F(4, 145) = 6.12, higher in the frequent group than in all others (P < 0.05). Delusions inventory total: 22.72 (14.10) frequent, 15.1 (10.33) infrequent, 15.79 (11.47) ex-ketamine, 13.03 (9.17) polydrug, 9.43 (9.21) non-drug (F(4, 145) = 8.40), reported as higher in the frequent group than in all others (P < 0.05) and in the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups than in the non-drug group (P < 0.01). Dissociative experiences: 784 (451), 630 (408), 401 (264), 488 (325), 321 (267) (F(4, 145) = 6.60), higher in the frequent group than in all except the infrequent group, and in the infrequent than in the non-drug group. Editors' recalculation from Table 6 (pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): delusions F ≈ 5.9, frequent against polydrug P ≈ 0.008 and against non-drug P < 0.001, but infrequent and ex-ketamine against non-drug P ≈ 0.48 and 0.27; dissociation F ≈ 8.3, frequent against polydrug P ≈ 0.014 and against non-drug P < 0.001.

evidence.locator: Results › Beck Depression Inventory (Table 6), Speilberger Trait Anxiety scale (Table 6) and Correlations, 1st paragraph (p. 84); Discussion › Psychological wellbeing, 3rd paragraph (p. 85)
evidence.extracted: Beck Depression Inventory: 11.48 (8.17) frequent, 9.03 (6.10) infrequent, 6.00 (5.11) ex-ketamine, 7.17 (5.38) polydrug, 7.23 (7.00) non-drug (F(4, 145) = 3.04, P = 0.019), reported as higher in the frequent group than in all others (P < 0.05); the Discussion calls the frequent group's mean mild to moderate depression and suggests people may be treating existing depression with ketamine. Trait anxiety did not differ. In the frequent group the delusions inventory total correlated with the current amount used per session (r = 0.433, P = 0.019). Editors' recalculation from Table 6 (pooled SD, Bonferroni): the frequent group's depression score differs from the ex-ketamine group's (P ≈ 0.01) but not from the polydrug or non-drug groups' (P ≈ 0.11 and 0.12).

evidence.locator: Method › Participants, 1st paragraph, and Procedure, 1st paragraph (p. 78); Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph, and Table 1 (p. 80); Discussion › Psychological wellbeing, 1st paragraph (p. 85); Limitations, 1st paragraph (p. 86)
evidence.extracted: Groups of 30: frequent ketamine use (more than four times a week), infrequent use (less than four times a week but at least once a month), ex-ketamine (abstinent for at least 1 month), polydrug and non-drug controls. Family history of mental illness was more common in the frequent group (8 of 30 against 2, 3, 1 and 1 in the other groups; χ²(4) = 12.59, P = 0.013), with no first-degree relative with schizophrenia in any group, and the frequent group had 12.27 (4.84) years of education against 14.23 to 15.33. The authors state that pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out, that the family history may have contributed to the findings, and that childhood trauma, a risk factor for dissociation, was not measured.

evidence.locator: Table 4 and Results › Psychological wellbeing (Table 4) › PDI (Fig. 1) and BDI (p. 128); DES (p. 129)
evidence.extracted: A year later in the same cohort, delusions inventory (number of items endorsed) at the first session and at follow-up: frequent 8.39 (3.30) and 8.04 (4.24), infrequent 6.92 and 6.62, abstinent 7.00 and 6.52, polydrug 5.63 and 4.50, non-drug 3.90 and 3.95; group effect F(4,108) = 4.16 (printed P = 0.04), with the frequent (P < 0.001), infrequent (P = 0.009) and abstinent groups (P = 0.016) above the non-drug group and the frequent above the polydrug group (P = 0.002). Dissociative experiences: group effect F(4,106) = 4.69, P = 0.002, the frequent group above the polydrug (P = 0.015) and non-drug groups (P = 0.009) (frequent 76.95 and 75.09). Depression: group × time F(4,110) = 2.97, P = 0.022, rising in the frequent (7.08 to 10.67, P = 0.041) and abstinent groups (4.96 to 9.00, P = 0.013), while the infrequent group's fell (10.04 to 8.08).

evidence.locator: Results › Demographics (Table 1), 1st paragraph (p. 124); Table 4 (p. 128); Results › LES (p. 129)
evidence.extracted: The frequent group's completers started at a depression score of 7.08 (5.27); the frequent group reported more negative life events over the year than the infrequent, polydrug and non-drug groups (F(4,104) = 4.30, P = 0.003), and had fewer years of education than the infrequent and abstinent groups (12.2 against 15.23 and 15.24; P < 0.05). Editors' comparison: the earlier report of the same session gives 11.48 for all 30 frequent participants, which implies a mean of about 33 in the 5 not retested, or an inconsistency between the two papers (card sc_morgan_2010b).

evidence.locator: Methods › Assessments › Dissociation and schizotypal symptomatology, and Mood and subjective effects › Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (p. 579); Results › Demographics and drug use › Reported general drug use (p. 580, right column); Table 2 (p. 581); Results › Dissociation and schizotypal symptomatology (Table 2) (p. 584, continuing on p. 585); Mood and somatic measures › Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (p. 585)
evidence.extracted: Three days after a night of use, the ketamine group, which reported using ketamine from twice a week (12%) to once a month (12%), rated dissociation 17.75 (17.41) against 5.37 (7.21) (p<0.008) and state schizotypal symptoms 62.35 (25.35) against 26.42 (20.45) (p<0.001), with magical ideation 28.25 against 11.00, compared with peers with little or no ketamine use, whose scores correlated highly across the two days (r = 0.93 and 0.94), although their mean schizotypal score fell from 33.37 to 26.42; both scales rate the current state. Depression on the anxiety and depression questionnaire was 4.45 (2.11) against 1.89 (1.29) on the night, a rating that covered the previous two days, and 4.30 (2.58) against 1.68 (1.29) three days later (group F(1,32) = 19.4), which the authors call low and well below the clinically significant range of 8–11.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Dissociative, psychotogenic and subjective effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors note that the schizotypal questionnaire was devised for this study and not validated, that its items tap psychosis proneness rather than psychoticism in a clinical sense, and that their data cannot tell a cumulative or residual effect of ketamine from pre-existing differences in dissociation and schizotypy.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 754); Results › Dissociation and schizotypal symptomatology (Table 3) (p. 755); Table 3 (p. 756); Table 4 (p. 757); Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 758)
evidence.extracted: Three days after use, dissociation (4.56 (6.35) against 3.47 (5.56)) and state schizotypal scores (25.28 (19.80) against 28.95 (21.37)) did not differ between people using ketamine more than twice a month (a reported 13.53 days a month) and people using it twice a month or less (0.45 days a month); the authors' hypothesis of more residual psychotogenic and dissociative symptoms with frequent use was not confirmed. The more frequent group's depression rating on day 3 was 20.39 (25.19) against 10.21 (11.04), with no test reported. Editors' calculation: t(35) = 1.61, p ≈ 0.12 for that rating.

evidence.locator: Results › Demographics (Table 1), 1st paragraph, and Table 1 (p. 1454); Table 4 (p. 1455); Subjective measures (Table 4) › Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire and Adapted Dissociative States Scale (p. 1456); Discussion › Subjective effects, 1st paragraph, and Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph (p. 1459)
evidence.extracted: Among 18 people who had cut down and 10 polydrug controls, state schizotypal symptoms were higher in the ketamine group at both sessions (51.5 (21.28) against 24.8 (8.16) three days after a night of use; 18.67 (17.05) against 4.0 (4.06) three to four years later; group F(1,26) = 15.32, P = 0.001) and fell in both groups; dissociation did not differ (10.11 against 5.44, then 3.24 against 0.80); at follow-up depression on the anxiety and depression questionnaire was higher (5.27 (4.32) against 2.00 (2.45); U = 55.5, P < 0.031 as printed; editors' calculation: U = 55.5 for groups of 18 and 10 gives a two-tailed p of about 0.10), which the authors say was not within a clinical range; schizotypal scores did not correlate with ketamine use. Editors' note: the same page says the earlier field study's participants did not differ from controls on depression at baseline, which contradicts that paper's own report of higher depression scores in its ketamine group (Curran & Morgan, 2000, p. 585).

evidence.locator: Method, 1st paragraph (p. 1452); Discussion › Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (p. 1459)
evidence.extracted: One member of the original ketamine groups had developed schizophrenia by the time of follow-up and was excluded from the analysed sample; the Discussion presents this case as anecdotal evidence and says it is not clear whether the higher schizotypal scores reflect pre-existing differences or chronic effects of ketamine.

evidence.locator: Chronic physical and psychological effects of ketamine › Depression, 1st paragraph (p. 31, continuing on p. 32); Psychosis, 2nd paragraph (p. 32)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review (second-hand, by two of the same authors): the rise in depression scores over the one-year study was not at clinical levels and did not correlate with changes in ketamine use; scores on measures of delusions, dissociation and schizotypy were higher with daily than with infrequent use and with infrequent use than in polydrug controls (citing the one-year study and the first field study); there is no evidence of clinical psychotic symptoms with infrequent use, and, despite anecdotes, little evidence of a link between chronic heavy use and a diagnosed psychotic disorder.

risk_of_bias.note: Family history of mental illness and education differ and are not adjusted for; all outcomes are self-ratings, some on scales built or adapted for the studies; testers knew the groups; samples are self-selected volunteers; several reported post hoc differences, and the 3-year follow-up's depression test, cannot be reproduced from the printed figures, and the frequent group's depression at the first session differs between the 2009 and 2010 papers (cards sc_morgan_2009, sc_morgan_2010b: ROBINS-E high; sc_curran_2000, sc_curran_2001, sc_morgan_2004a: very high).

inconsistency.note: Delusion-like beliefs and depressive symptoms point the same way in every comparison with people who did not use ketamine, but dissociation was raised in some comparisons and not in others (no difference after cutting down; none between frequent and less frequent use three days after a night out), and the depression differences are fragile.

indirectness.note: The outcomes are the self-rated experiences asked about; none of the scales is a diagnosis, which the claim states.

imprecision.note: 10 to 30 people per group; differences at the limit of significance for depression, with intervals that would include small differences.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all studies are from one group.

dose_response.note: The ordering of delusional ideation across groups (frequent above infrequent and abstinent, above the controls) and its correlation with amount per session in the frequent group (r = 0.433, one of an unstated number of correlations) are suggestive, but frequent against infrequent use was not tested in the one-year data and the groups differ in family history; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low. Overlapping evidence: Morgan et al. (2009) and (2010b) are the same participants and count once; the 3-year follow-up (Morgan et al., 2004a) is a subset of the two field studies' participants, so the field studies and the follow-up are not independent of each other; the narrative review (Morgan & Curran, 2012) is second-hand and only qualifies. Status replicated by the same team: in every sample of this one group that included people who did not use ketamine, people who used it scored higher on delusion-like or psychosis-like scales and on depressive symptoms than those who did not (the depression differences are fragile), while the dissociation findings are less consistent. Rated as worded, an association; the editors draw no causal conclusion.
